claim_1.claim: Transcription profiling by array analysis of pre-vaccination whole blood from the EM131 elderly cohort (age≥65) showed that a higher BioAge signature, particularly lower expression of B-cell module M1 (including CD79A, CD79B, CD19, CD22, POU2AF1 and MZB1) and higher expression of inflammatory module M16 (including C1, MYD88, IRF7, LILRA5, S100, IL15, PILRA and PRELID1), was associated with poorer HBV vaccine response measured 1 month after the second Twinrix vaccination [absolute day not stated].

sources.quote: Both the BioAge score (Supplementary Fig. 3) and the two groups of elderly identified by the BioAge signature (Fisher's exact test: odds ratio (OR)=2.14, P=0.0357; Fig. 3a) were associated with the rate of response to the HBV vaccine.

Among the 20 gene modules defined in the BioAge signature, 2 modules M1 (lower expression in BioAge old) and M16 (high expression in BioAge old) allowed the most accurate prediction of the response to the HBV vaccine (Fig. 3b).

Pathway enrichment analysis showed that module M1 was enriched in genes encoding two critical components of the B-cell receptor, that is, CD79A and CD79B, B-cell activation markers such as CD19, CD22, the transcription factor POU2AF1 (a protein essential for the response of B cells to antigens and required for the formation of germinal centres)22 and MZB-1, a chaperone involved in assembly of IgM23 (Fig. 3c). Module M16 includes genes of the acute phase response, that is, the complement gene C1, the mediator of type II interferon response MYD88 and the transcription factor IRF7. IRF7 target genes such as LILRA5 (a marker expressed by TNF-producing macrophages), S100 (a molecule associated to cellular senescence), IL-15 (a pro-inflammatory cytokine that triggers CD8 T-cell and NK-cell expansion), PILRA (an inhibitory receptor that acts through SHP-1) and PRELID-1 (a gene that negatively regulates the development of TH2 responses) were also present in module M16 (Fig. 3c).
To identify pre-vaccination biomarkers of vaccine response, the data set was restricted to pre-vaccination samples (138/280 samples).
Though HBV titres were measured 1 month after the second dose, all patients were offered the third dose to conform to the approved regimen.

comparison.finding: elderly with a higher BioAge signature had poorer HBV vaccine response than elderly with a lower BioAge signature; the higher BioAge subgroup was characterized by lower expression of B-cell module M1 (CD79A, CD79B, CD19, CD22, POU2AF1, MZB1) and higher expression of inflammatory module M16 (C1, MYD88, IRF7, LILRA5, S100, IL15, PILRA, PRELID1)

claim_2.claim: Transcription profiling by array analysis of pre-vaccination whole blood from elderly participants in the EM131 training and test sets showed that a 15-gene signature predicted HBV vaccine responders versus poor-responders measured 1 month after the second Twinrix vaccination [absolute day not stated], with 62.6% accuracy in 10-fold cross-validation on the training set and 62.2% accuracy on the test set; the signature included B-cell-related genes such as CD20, IGHG1 and BANK1 and inflammatory genes including C1, FCGR3B and HP.

sources.quote: We then tested if a combination of genes (multivariate model) could distinguish the two classes of responders. To that end, a naive Bayes classifier based on the top 15 differentially expressed genes between responders and poor-responders to the HBV vaccines was built on the EM131 training set (Fig. 4a).

The accuracy of the resulting 15-gene signature was assessed on the EM131 training set by 10-fold cross-validation and on the EM131 test set and found to be 62.6% and 62.2%, respectively (Fig. 4b,c, Supplementary Fig. 4 and Supplementary Table 4b).

Network inference revealed that several members of this 15-gene signature included markers of B cells (for example, CD20, IGHG1), as well as downstream targets of B-cell receptor signalling (for example, BANK1) and molecules known to have functional interactions with IgG (for example, C1, FCGR3B; Fig. 4d).
In the 15-gene signature, haptoglobin (HP), an acute phase protein and also a target gene of type I interferon signalling, was associated with low Ab titres.

To identify pre-vaccination biomarkers of vaccine response, the data set was restricted to pre-vaccination samples (138/280 samples). The resulting training set and test set contained 91 and 47 samples, respectively (Supplementary Table 1).

Participants who had anti-HBsAg titres 1 month after the second immunization below detection threshold (<5 mIU ml−1) were considered poor-responders to the HBV vaccine (n=52), while participants with anti-HBsAg titres ≥5 mIU ml−1 were considered responders to the HBV vaccine (n=38).

comparison.finding: A 15-gene pre-vaccination signature distinguished HBV vaccine responders from poor-responders, with 62.6% accuracy in 10-fold cross-validation on the EM131 training set and 62.2% accuracy on the test set; signature genes included CD20, IGHG1, BANK1, C1, FCGR3B, and HP, with HP associated with low antibody titres.

claim_3.claim: ELISA analysis of serum from 174 pre-vaccination EM131 samples showed that higher baseline inflammatory proteins IL-15, IL-1ra and TNFR2 in the training set were negatively associated with HBV vaccine response measured 1 month after the second Twinrix vaccination [absolute day not stated], but the resulting 3-cytokine model was not significantly associated with response in the test set (permutation test P=0.250).

sources.quote: We also screened a panel of 47 serum cytokines and chemokines for their association with the response to HBV vaccination. Three inflammation-associated proteins—IL-15, IL-1ra and TNFR2—were negatively associated with HBV vaccine response on the EM131 training set (Supplementary Table 5b,c and Supplementary Fig. 5b).
This model was not significantly associated to the HBV vaccine response in the EM131 test set (Supplementary Fig. 5c, permutation test: P=0.250).

A panel of 45 cytokines/chemokines was measured on the 174 pre-vaccination (V2) samples of the EM131 cohort. Samples were assayed to determine the concentration of inflammatory proteins according to multianalyte profiling protocols established by Rules-Based Medicine (RBM) (Austin, TX). Serum samples were shipped to RBM for analysis using the multiplex ELISA protocol Human Inflammation multianalyte profiling (Supplementary Table 5b).
Though HBV titres were measured 1 month after the second dose, all patients were offered the third dose to conform to the approved regimen.

comparison.finding: In the EM131 training set, higher baseline IL-15, IL-1ra and TNFR2 were negatively associated with HBV vaccine response, but the resulting 3-cytokine model was not significantly associated with response in the EM131 test set (permutation test P=0.250).
